newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WEIBRING, WIEBE LEAD LEHMAN, NORMAN AT KEMPER OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WEIBRING, WIEBE LEAD LEHMAN, NORMAN AT KEMPER OPEN.

text.p: D.A. Weibring, still struggling with his health more than a year after contracting a debilitating virus, shot a four-under-par 67 Friday to tie for the lead after the second round of the Kemper Open.
An eagle at the par-four 14th was just what the doctor ordered for Weibring, who shared the second-round lead with fellow-American Mark Wiebe at six-under 136 at Avenel TPC.
Wiebe also shot 67 as the co-leaders stood one shot ahead of British Open champion Tom Lehman (69), Omar Uresti (69), John Morse (68) and joint first-round leader Greg Norman (71).
The other first-round leader, Nick Price, had a 72 to slip two strokes behind in a group that included Nick Faldo, who had the day's best round, a flawless 65.
Weibring, whose initials stand for Donald Albert, was stricken in February last year by Bell's palsy, a virus which caused temporary paralysis of the right side of his face.
He took more than a month off, and even though he bounced back to win the Greater Hartford Open in June, the illness took a lot out of him.
"Even though I was blessed to win, there was a passion missing. I really got worn down at the end of the year," admitted Weibring, who is 158th on this year's PGA Tour money list.
"I have not fully got rid of the Bell's palsy. I feel soreness in my cheek and a flickering around my eye. I have to wear sunglasses from time to time. It's something I have to deal with."
Even if he wins here, Weibring will not play in next week's U.S. Open after failing to qualify.
Wiebe, on the other hand, is in the U.S. Open field after surviving 36-hole qualifying on Tuesday. Like Weibring, he also has battled with his health recently.
"I've been going through a bad time for two months with allergies," said Wiebe, who is receiving two injections weekly.
"I'm allergic to trees, specifically oak, elm and cottonwood, as well as grass. Bermuda (grass) is my worst allergy."
Wiebe had four birdies in a bogey-free round, no mean feat considering how difficult most of the players found putting on the sub-standard greens.
"The greens are pretty tough to putt. You have to hit your putts solid. You'd think we'd always hit our putts solid, but we don't," he said.
The condition of the greens perhaps explained why the field was so bunched. Only seven strokes separated the 70 players who made the cut.
Last week's winner, Vijay Singh of Fiji, stood at one-over 143, making the cut for a 37th consecutive event on the PGA Tour, the current longest streak.
